entries.why: DROP TABLE permanently destroys the table and every row it holds -- the floor operation D-02 protects, and the first fixture the corpus manifest schema and harness are built against.
DROP SCHEMA permanently destroys every object inside the schema, including all of its tables and their data.
DROP DATABASE permanently destroys the entire database, every schema and table in it.
TRUNCATE removes every row from a table in a single unrecoverable operation, bypassing per-row triggers and any WHERE-based scoping.
DROP COLUMN permanently destroys every value stored in that column across every row.
A DELETE with no WHERE clause removes every row in the table, which is almost never the intended scope of a migration.
An UPDATE with no WHERE clause overwrites every row in the table, which is almost never the intended scope of a migration.

CR-02 regression (03-REVIEW.md): PostgreSQL's own grammar allows more than one subcommand in a single ALTER TABLE, and inspectAlterTableStmt used to inspect only the first (cmds[0]), silently discarding every later subcommand before it ever reached classification. This fixture combines a harmless ADD COLUMN with a genuinely destructive DROP COLUMN in one statement -- before the fix, analyzeSql returned file verdict SAFE with a single finding for the ADD COLUMN, and the DROP COLUMN never appeared anywhere in the result. The fix must produce one finding per subcommand and the file verdict must be BLOCKED, worst-verdict-wins.

WR-01 regression (04-REVIEW.md): PostgreSQL's own grammar allows more than one object in a single DROP statement, and inspectDropStmt used to read only objects[0], silently discarding every later object before it ever reached classification -- the same bug shape CR-02 already fixed for multi-subcommand ALTER TABLE. This fixture drops two tables in one statement; the fix must produce one finding per object (test/multi-object-drop.test.ts's own length-2 assertion covers this directly, since both objects share the same drop-table rule id and the corpus harness's set-based expectedRuleIds comparison would not by itself catch a regression that dropped one of the two findings).

D-17/Pitfall 4 (04-RESEARCH.md): RESET ALL disarms lock_timeout and statement_timeout along with every other session GUC, but its AST node (VariableSetStmt, kind VAR_RESET_ALL) carries no name field at all -- a name-matching rule would miss it entirely. disarms-timeout-guc catches it because setstmtDisarmsTimeout treats VAR_RESET_ALL as unconditionally disarming, with no name check.

ALTER SYSTEM SET statement_timeout = 0 disarms the timeout cluster-wide, persisting across every future connection until reloaded -- D-17's floor makes this BLOCKED with no rules-file override, same as any other disarming form.

ALTER DATABASE ... SET lock_timeout = 0 disarms the timeout for every future session connecting to that database, persisting beyond the migration's own session -- exactly why Task 2's checkpoint decision (cover-all-scopes) floors the database- and role-scoped forms rather than recording them as a gap: they are the MORE dangerous forms of the same act, not a lesser one.

An ordinary session-level SET that does not touch lock_timeout or statement_timeout is not a floor violation, but it is not nothing either -- set-guc-non-timeout gives it a named REVIEW_REQUIRED rule id instead of falling through to the Unrecognized default, distinguishing 'a SET the catalogue has an opinion on' from 'a statement kind the catalogue has never seen.'

The positive half of criterion 2: a standalone CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY on a real recipe-core column (recipes.slug) is the statement the runner must be able to execute unwrapped -- transactionHostile true, but that is not itself a hazard the classifier flags; the existing create-index-concurrently rule already grants SAFE, so no duplicate rule row was added (rules.json's own notes field records this).

VACUUM cannot run inside a transaction block and can hold locks or scan large tables for a long time depending on options and table size, so vacuum-in-migration gives it a named REVIEW_REQUIRED rule id rather than falling through to the Unrecognized default.

CREATE DATABASE cannot run inside a transaction block and creates a whole new database outside the schema this migration pipeline otherwise governs, so create-database-in-migration gives it a named REVIEW_REQUIRED rule id rather than falling through to the Unrecognized default.

A non-concurrent REINDEX takes ACCESS EXCLUSIVE on the indexed table for the whole rebuild, blocking reads and writes until it finishes, so reindex-in-migration gives it a named REVIEW_REQUIRED rule id rather than falling through to the Unrecognized default.
SET NOT NULL on an existing column forces a full table scan under ACCESS EXCLUSIVE -- the canonical lock-hazard REVIEW REQUIRED case.
clock_timestamp() is genuinely volatile -- a different value on every call -- so PostgreSQL cannot store it as a single metadata entry and must rewrite the whole table.
ALTER COLUMN TYPE always takes ACCESS EXCLUSIVE, and this analyzer has no database connection to tell a safe widening from a lossy narrowing, so the question goes to a human.
Adding a UNIQUE constraint without USING INDEX builds its backing index while holding ACCESS EXCLUSIVE for the entire build, blocking reads and writes.
Building an index without CONCURRENTLY takes a SHARE lock on the table for the whole build, blocking every INSERT, UPDATE and DELETE until it finishes.
Dropping an index without CONCURRENTLY takes ACCESS EXCLUSIVE on the table for the drop, which can queue behind and then block every other lock request on it.
A plainly added foreign key scans and locks both the altering table and the referenced table while validating every existing row, unlike the NOT VALID plus VALIDATE CONSTRAINT two-step form.
Renaming a column is an instant metadata change with no lock hazard, but any application code still referencing the old name breaks immediately during a rolling deploy's compatibility window.
Renaming a table is an instant metadata change with no lock hazard, but any application code still referencing the old name breaks immediately during a rolling deploy's compatibility window.
Dropping a NOT NULL constraint is metadata-only with no lock hazard, but it silently changes what application code can rely on being present.
Dropping a constraint is metadata-only with no lock hazard, but whether any application code depends on the guarantee it enforced is an application-level fact this analyzer cannot verify.

generate_external_ref() is absent from the curated function-volatility table, so its defaultVolatility is unknown-function and no rule matches -- D-06's 'SAFE must be earned' proven for a default the analyzer genuinely cannot classify, never guessed SAFE by omission.

CREATE SEQUENCE is a perfectly ordinary, harmless PostgreSQL statement the catalogue has no rule for at all -- it resolves to statementKind Unrecognized and D-06's no-match default, proving an unfamiliar-but-harmless statement stops for a human instead of sailing through as SAFE by default.
Creating a brand new table has no existing rows to lock, scan or rewrite and no application code can yet depend on it -- the simplest SAFE case.
Adding a nullable column with no default is a metadata-only change that requires no table rewrite and no scan of existing rows.
A literal default is evaluated once and stored in the table's own metadata, so PostgreSQL's fast add-column path applies and no rewrite is required.

now() is catalogued STABLE, not VOLATILE (03-RESEARCH.md's Pitfall 1 correction) -- it is evaluated once at ALTER TABLE time and stored in metadata exactly like a literal, so PostgreSQL's fast add-column path applies. Expecting REVIEW_REQUIRED here would be a false positive on a genuinely safe migration, the exact review-fatigue anti-pattern this catalogue exists to avoid; its counterpart (a clock_timestamp() default, review-required/add-column-volatile-default.sql) is genuinely VOLATILE and correctly expects REVIEW_REQUIRED -- the two fixtures together make the STABLE-vs-VOLATILE distinction visible in the corpus, not only in a unit test.
CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY takes only SHARE UPDATE EXCLUSIVE, letting concurrent reads and writes continue for almost the entire build.
DROP INDEX CONCURRENTLY takes only SHARE UPDATE EXCLUSIVE, letting concurrent reads and writes continue for almost the entire drop.
COMMENT ON only updates catalog metadata text, taking no meaningful lock and touching no row in the table it describes.
A check constraint added NOT VALID is instant and enforces only on new or changed rows, deferring the table scan to a separate, weaker-locked VALIDATE CONSTRAINT step.
A foreign key added NOT VALID is instant and enforces only on new or changed rows, deferring the scan of both tables to a separate, weaker-locked VALIDATE CONSTRAINT step.

VALIDATE CONSTRAINT takes only SHARE UPDATE EXCLUSIVE on the altered table, letting concurrent reads and writes continue while it scans for constraint violations -- true on its own regardless of what statement (if any) preceded it in the same file.

The complete two-step safe form for adding a validated constraint without a table-scanning lock: a check constraint added NOT VALID, then validated by its own VALIDATE CONSTRAINT naming the exact same constraint on the exact same table in this same file -- the applySafeFormPairing pass adds pair-not-valid-validated to both statements' findings alongside each half's own already-SAFE rule id.

The complete two-step safe form for adding a unique constraint without blocking writes during the index build: an index built CONCURRENTLY, then attached via ADD CONSTRAINT ... UNIQUE USING INDEX naming that exact index -- without the pairing, the second statement would be an unmatched D-06 REVIEW_REQUIRED (no ordinary rule matches AddUniqueConstraint with a non-null usingIndexName), so pair-concurrent-index-unique is the only thing that resolves it to SAFE.

The complete three-step safe form for enforcing NOT NULL without an ACCESS EXCLUSIVE scan: a CHECK (col IS NOT NULL) constraint added NOT VALID, validated (itself pairing via pair-not-valid-validated), then SET NOT NULL on that same column -- PostgreSQL 12+ detects the validated check constraint and skips SET NOT NULL's own table scan, which pair-validated-check-set-not-null is what lowers the naive REVIEW_REQUIRED set-not-null finding to SAFE.

Near-miss control proving the pairing match is exact name equality, never a fuzzy or approximate match: an index built CONCURRENTLY as orders_customer_id_idx, paired against a unique constraint whose USING INDEX names a DIFFERENT index (orders_other_idx) -- one character or one whole word different is still a different index, not a typo to forgive, so pair-concurrent-index-unique never fires and the constraint statement falls through to D-06's unmatched REVIEW_REQUIRED. (The literal 'unvalidated-then-validate pair with a mismatched constraint name' shape the plan text originally described does NOT produce this outcome under the real analyzer -- see 03-05-SUMMARY.md's Deviations section for why this shape was substituted.)

CR-02's completeness counterpart: two subcommands in one ALTER TABLE, both harmless nullable ADD COLUMNs with no default. Proves the multi-subcommand fix produces a finding for EVERY subcommand (not just the first, and not just when one is dangerous) -- both findings carry the same add-column-nullable-no-default rule id, so the corpus harness's set-based expectedRuleIds comparison would not by itself catch a regression that dropped one of the two identical findings; test/multi-subcommand-alter-table.test.ts's own length-2 assertion covers that gap directly.

D-14/PITFALLS.md C1: a block comment sits between the DROP TABLE keyword and the table name, inside the statement itself -- the statement still executes exactly as written. A line-oriented text scan that treats anything after -- or between /* */ as inert would miss this; the real parser strips the comment and sees a genuine DropTable node regardless.

D-14's false-positive half, the one PITFALLS.md C2 warns rots first: a leading line comment mentions dropping the table in prose, but the actual statement is an ordinary nullable ADD COLUMN. A regex matching 'drop' in a comment would flag this; the real parser only sees the SQL statement, never the comment text.

D-14/PITFALLS.md C1: the real drop lives inside a dollar-quoted function body using a custom tag ($migration_body$, not the default $$) -- proving the recursion (D-05) re-parses the body regardless of which dollar tag was used to quote it, and the container itself still earns its own SAFE finding (bodyInspected true) alongside the nested BLOCKED one (D-10: complete findings list, worst verdict wins).

D-14's false-positive half: the words DROP TABLE orders appear only as DATA -- a dollar-quoted string literal (custom tag $evasion_tag$, proving tagged quoting specifically) being inserted as an ordinary column value. INSERT has no StatementKind in this catalogue at all (D-04 never included it, same limitation 03-04/03-05 already documented), so this resolves REVIEW_REQUIRED via D-06's unmatched-statement default -- never BLOCKED, and no drop rule id anywhere in its findings.

D-14/PITFALLS.md C1: the drop is guarded by real control flow (an IF around it, deciding at runtime whether to run), not sitting at the top of the body -- extractEmbeddedSql's deep generic tree walk (not a named-construct allowlist) finds it regardless of which branch it is nested inside, exactly the standard PITFALLS.md C1's IF-guarded-DROP example demands.

D-14's false-positive half: the body only raises a NOTICE whose message text mentions not dropping the table -- RAISE is not PLpgSQL_stmt_execsql/dynexecute, so extractEmbeddedSql's walk finds no embedded SQL at all, and the container earns its own SAFE finding (bodyInspected true) with no nested finding and no drop rule id.

D-14/PITFALLS.md C1's 'CREATE OR REPLACE FUNCTION bodies' bullet: a LANGUAGE sql function whose body is a single-quoted (not dollar-quoted) string containing a real DROP TABLE -- the post-03-04 gap-closure fix's own LANGUAGE sql re-parse path (planContainerBody's sql-text branch, never parsePlPgSQL) catches it exactly like the plpgsql case, proving the evasion fails regardless of which quoting style hides the body.

D-14's false-positive half: a LANGUAGE sql function whose body only returns a string constant mentioning dropping the table, never an executable drop. The container earns its own SAFE finding (bodyInspected true), but the body's own SELECT statement has no StatementKind in this catalogue (SELECT was never in D-04's scope), so the nested finding is REVIEW_REQUIRED via D-06's unmatched default -- worst-verdict-wins makes the file REVIEW_REQUIRED, never BLOCKED, and no drop rule id anywhere.

D-14/PITFALLS.md C1: the table being dropped is literally named "table" (a double-quoted identifier colliding with a SQL keyword) -- proving that quoting an identifier to look unusual does not change what statement it is: this is still a genuine DropStmt node, and drop-table matches on statementKind alone, never on the literal text of the name.

D-14's false-positive half: a table is CREATED whose quoted name is itself the phrase "drop table" -- proving an identifier that reads like an entire dangerous statement is not treated as one. This is a genuine CreateStmt node classified SAFE by create-table; nothing about the identifier's text is ever inspected.

D-17's nested coverage rides on D-05's existing recursion: a DO block whose body genuinely executes SET lock_timeout = '0' before an ALTER TABLE ADD COLUMN is still caught one level down, live-verified via analyzeSql -- the container itself earns its own SAFE finding (bodyInspected true), the disarming SET earns disarms-timeout-guc at sourceContext do-block, and the harmless ADD COLUMN earns its own SAFE finding, with worst-verdict-wins making the whole file BLOCKED.

D-17's false-positive half: the exact words 'SET lock_timeout = ''0'';' appear only inside a -- comment and inside a dollar-quoted string literal ($msg$...$msg$) passed to RAISE NOTICE, never executed as a SET statement -- extractEmbeddedSql finds no PLpgSQL_stmt_execsql/dynexecute in the body (RAISE is neither), so no disarms-timeout-guc finding appears anywhere; live-verified via analyzeSql to classify SAFE via the container's own SAFE finding plus a genuinely harmless top-level ADD COLUMN, proving comments and inert string data are inert exactly as this project's own stated purpose requires.

D-16: mirrors 01-CONTEXT.md D-11's reserved 'nullable notes column' churn on the real recipes table without touching apps/recipe-app/src/db/schema.ts -- a metadata-only ADD COLUMN with no default requires no table rewrite and no scan, so Phase 4 already knows this lands SAFE before spending the real change.

D-16: mirrors 01-CONTEXT.md D-11's reserved churn by enforcing NOT NULL on the real, existing nullable steps.timer_label column directly (the naive one-liner, not the NOT VALID/VALIDATE/SET NOT NULL three-step form) -- PITFALLS.md A5's canonical lock hazard: SET NOT NULL must scan the whole table under ACCESS EXCLUSIVE to prove no existing row violates the constraint, which the analyzer has no database connection to skip, so this correctly lands REVIEW_REQUIRED rather than SAFE.

D-16: mirrors 01-CONTEXT.md D-11's reserved churn -- dropping the real ingredients table, which both it and steps cascade-delete from recipes, is the closest thing this repository has to the actual disaster this whole project exists to prevent. The D-02 floor makes this BLOCKED unconditionally, with no rules-file override possible.

04-07/D-32: the REAL bytes `drizzle-kit generate` produced when `ingredients` and its relations were removed from schema.ts for real -- `DROP TABLE "ingredients" CASCADE;`, quoting the identifier and adding CASCADE, neither of which the Phase 3 hand-written mirror (drop-ingredients-table.sql, unquoted, no CASCADE) predicted verbatim. Run live through `pnpm db:migrate` against the real pinned development database: refused BLOCKED, rule drop-table, exit code 21 (RUNNER_EXIT_CODES.REFUSED_BLOCKED), zero ledger rows added, the live `ingredients` table and its 8 seeded rows confirmed still present afterward. The schema edit, the generated migration, and the journal entry were then fully reverted (git status --porcelain apps/recipe-app empty, journal byte-identical via git hash-object) -- this fixture is what makes that refusal permanent, regression-tested against the exact bytes drizzle actually produces rather than only the Phase 3 prediction.

The repository's first genuine Drizzle-generated migration, referenced in place rather than copied (the same bytes the runner would execute): a single CREATE TABLE statement for recipes. New tables have no existing rows to lock, scan or rewrite -- create-table matches unconditionally, regardless of the uuid/now() column defaults inside it, which only matter for ADD COLUMN, not table creation.

The repository's second genuine Drizzle migration, referenced in place: two CREATE TABLE statements (SAFE, create-table) followed by two ADD CONSTRAINT ... FOREIGN KEY statements with no NOT VALID flag. A plainly added foreign key scans and locks both the altering and the referenced table while validating every existing row (PITFALLS.md A6) -- a correct REVIEW_REQUIRED classification of real Drizzle-generated SQL, not a defect: the safe form would have added the constraint NOT VALID and validated it in a separate statement, which this migration does not do. Live-verified against the installed analyzer (a disposable probe script, then discarded) before being written here, per this plan's own corpus_integrity instruction to reason about correctness rather than copy an unexamined actual value.

04-06/D-30: the real, generated ADD COLUMN notes -- a metadata-only ADD COLUMN with no default requires no table rewrite and no scan, exactly matching the Phase 3 corpus prediction (app-shaped/recipes-add-notes-column.sql) checked against reality. Live-verified against the installed analyzer via `pnpm db:analyze` before being written here, and applied through `pnpm db:migrate` (verdict SAFE, exit 0).

04-06/D-31: the real, hand-authored backfill (a single scoped `UPDATE steps SET timer_label = '' WHERE timer_label IS NULL`) that must run before the SET NOT NULL migration, since the seed genuinely leaves NULL rows. It demonstrates the update-without-where floor rule from the PASSING side -- a scoped UPDATE matches no rule at all (D-06's unmatched-statement default applies, expectedRuleIds empty exactly like review-required/add-column-unknown-default-function.sql's own precedent), where the same statement without a WHERE would be BLOCKED. Live-verified against the installed analyzer via `pnpm db:analyze` and applied through `pnpm db:migrate` (verdict REVIEW_REQUIRED, exit 0).

04-06/D-31: the real, generated constraint migration (`SET DEFAULT ''` then `SET NOT NULL` on steps.timer_label) -- a full table scan under ACCESS EXCLUSIVE the analyzer has no connection to skip, matching the Phase 3 corpus prediction (app-shaped/steps-timer-label-set-not-null.sql) checked against reality. The SET DEFAULT statement matches no rule (D-06 unmatched default, contributing no rule id), so set-not-null is the only rule id the file's findings carry. Live-verified against the installed analyzer via `pnpm db:analyze` before being written here, and applied through `pnpm db:migrate` (verdict REVIEW_REQUIRED, exit 0).
